Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Pakistan's president has defended his government's recent ceasefire in the country's volatile Swat Valley in a Wall Street Journal opinion piece, saying that many in the West have mischaracterized the deal. President Zardari also said that the cease-fire would not close girls' schools in the troubled region. The permanent ceasefire, which was brokered in late February between members of the Taliban and leaders of Swat Valley, has been criticized and called a major concession by the Pakistani government in an attempt to hold off Taliban attacks. The central government has long exerted little control in the area, but it launched an intense military offensive in late July to flush out militants from areas of the North West Frontier Province . As retaliation for the military presence, the Taliban carried out a series of deadly attacks, beheadings and destruction of girls' schools. They also continued to gain ground, setting up checkpoints throughout the area. President Asif Ali Zardari addressed the international criticism in his Wall Street Journal article, published Wednesday. "We have not and will not negotiate with extremist Taliban and terrorists," Zardari wrote. "The clerics with whom we have engaged are not Taliban. Indeed, in our dialogue we'd made it clear that it is their responsibility to rein in and neutralize Taliban and other insurgents." The deal was brokered by Sufi Mohammed, a pro-Taliban cleric who in the past was arrested for leading thousands of fighters against the United States in Afghanistan. Mohammed made the deal with his son-in-law and Taliban commander Maulana Fazlullah. In the article, Zardari also said that the cease-fire would not close girls' schools in the region. "We have not and will not condone the closing of girls' schools, as we saw last year when militants closed schools in pockets of Swat Valley. Indeed, the government insists that the education of young women is mandatory. This is not an example of the government condoning or capitulating to extremism -- quite the opposite," Zardari wrote. The cease-fire deal imposes Islamic law, or sharia, in the region. As part of the agreement, the Taliban is allowing boys' schools to reopen and the government to set up temporary quarters for the more than 200,000 Swat residents who fled. Women in the area interviewed by CNN said that they would not be able to go to the schools and that, under Taliban-imposed sharia law, they cannot even be seen in public without their husbands or fathers. Swat Valley, located in North West Frontier Province, was once one of Pakistan's biggest tourist destinations. It is near the Afghanistan border and is 300 kilometers (186 miles) from the capital, Islamabad. -- CNN's Stan Grant contributed to this report.

**Zardari Defends Swat Valley Ceasefire Amid Western Criticism**

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan — President Asif Ali Zardari has mounted a vigorous defense of his government's controversial peace agreement with militants in the Swat Valley, pushing back against mounting criticism from Western allies who fear the deal signals a retreat in the fight against Islamist extremism.

The agreement, which effectively allows the implementation of Islamic law in the scenic northern valley in exchange for militants laying down their arms, has drawn sharp rebukes from Washington and European capitals. Critics argue the deal cedes territory to the Taliban-linked insurgency and could provide a haven for extremists near the Afghan border.

Speaking to reporters, Zardari insisted the ceasefire represents a pragmatic response to years of bloodshed that has devastated the region, once a popular tourist destination known for its mountain scenery.

"We have to look at the reality on the ground," Zardari said. "Years of military operations have not brought lasting peace to Swat. Our people are suffering. This agreement gives us a chance to restore normalcy and separate the local population from the militants who have terrorized them."

The deal, brokered with a pro-Taliban cleric, has raised alarm among U.S. officials who worry it mirrors previous failed truces in Pakistan's tribal areas that ultimately strengthened militant groups rather than weakening them. A senior State Department official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Washington had communicated its "serious concerns" to Islamabad through diplomatic channels.

Zardari pushed back firmly against suggestions that Pakistan was capitulating to extremists.

"This is not surrender," he said. "This is about giving peace a chance while we continue to fight terrorism where it threatens our state. We will not allow Swat or any part of Pakistan to become a sanctuary for those who wish to attack our people or destabilize our neighbors."

The president also appeared to bristle at what he characterized as Western nations second-guessing decisions made by Pakistan's democratically elected government.

"We understand the concerns of our international partners, but Pakistan's sovereignty and the safety of our citizens are our foremost responsibility," Zardari said. "We are the ones who have lost thousands of soldiers and civilians in this fight. We will not be lectured on how to achieve peace in our own country."

Analysts remain divided on the wisdom of the truce. Some argue that engaging local power brokers, rather than relying solely on military force, may be the only viable path to stability in Swat, where Pakistani forces have struggled for over a year to dislodge militants despite significant troop deployments.

Others warn the deal could embolden militant networks and further erode the writ of the Pakistani state in the region, potentially serving as a springboard for attacks elsewhere in the country.

The Swat Valley, once a haven for honeymooners and hikers, has been largely emptied of tourists since the insurgency took hold, with schools destroyed, government buildings targeted, and thousands of residents displaced by the fighting.

The Obama administration, which has made the fight against extremism in Pakistan and Afghanistan a top foreign policy priority, has signaled that continued U.S. support and aid to Pakistan could hinge on Islamabad demonstrating a credible strategy against militancy — a message that appeared to underscore the tension surrounding the Swat agreement.

Zardari, however, remained defiant, suggesting that Pakistan would chart its own course.

"We are committed partners in this fight against terrorism," he said, "but we will pursue the strategies that we believe will work best for our people and our country."

The situation in Swat continues to be closely watched as a bellwether for Pakistan's broader struggle to contain a growing insurgency that has increasingly threatened the stability of the nuclear-armed nation.

# Peace Deal in Swat Valley Sparks Fears Over Women's Rights, Education

**ISLAMABAD** — A controversial peace agreement between the Pakistani government and militant groups in the Swat Valley has ignited fierce debate over whether the accord represents a pragmatic path to stability or a dangerous capitulation that could reverse hard-won gains for women and education in the region.

President Asif Ali Zardari has defended the agreement, which allows for the implementation of Islamic law, or Sharia, in the Malakand region that includes Swat, as a necessary measure to restore order after nearly two years of violence that has left the valley in ruins.

"We had to make a choice between the lesser of two evils," Zardari said in remarks defending the deal. "Our priority is to bring peace to the region and to protect the lives of the people who have suffered enormously."

Government officials argue that the accord, negotiated with a pro-Taliban cleric who has served as an intermediary with militant commanders, offers the best chance to halt the bloodshed and create conditions for the eventual restoration of state authority.

## A Region Transformed

But on the ground, the reality for many residents—particularly women and girls—tells a starkly different story.

Once known as the "Switzerland of Pakistan" for its scenic beauty and relative prosperity, Swat has been transformed by years of insurgency into a landscape marked by fear and deprivation. Militants have destroyed or damaged hundreds of schools, with girls' education facilities disproportionately targeted. Local residents describe a climate in which women are increasingly barred from public life, markets have been threatened, and music, television, and other forms of entertainment have been banned in areas under militant influence.

Teachers and education activists say the peace deal does little to guarantee that girls' schools—many reduced to rubble—will reopen safely. "We are told this agreement will bring calm," one local resident said, speaking on condition of anonymity. "But calm for whom? The gunmen still patrol the streets. Girls are still afraid to go to class."

Human rights organizations have voiced alarm that the arrangement effectively cedes governance to militant-aligned clerics, warning that formalizing Sharia courts in the region could entrench restrictions on women without any enforceable safeguards for their rights.

## Political Fallout

Critics in Pakistan's parliament and civil society have accused the government of capitulating to extremism, arguing that the deal sets a dangerous precedent that could embolden militant groups elsewhere in the country's northwest.

Zardari has pushed back against such characterizations, insisting the government retains ultimate authority and describing the arrangement as a homegrown solution reflecting the wishes of local residents desperate for an end to violence.

"This is not a surrender," he said. "It is an attempt to give people a chance to live without the fear of bombs and bullets, so that we can then work to restore full government writ."

Skeptics, however, note that similar agreements in the past have collapsed within months, providing militants breathing room to regroup rather than any lasting peace. With international observers watching closely, the durability of the Swat accord—and its human cost—remains very much in question.

*This report is based on developments as of early 2009, when the peace agreement was signed amid intense scrutiny from both domestic and international observers.*

# Pakistan's Uneasy Peace: Government Defends Swat Valley Ceasefire Amid Sharia Law Deal

**ISLAMABAD** — Pakistan's government has moved to defend a controversial ceasefire agreement with pro-Taliban clerics in the Swat Valley, framing the deal—which paves the way for the implementation of Islamic law in the region—as a pragmatic step toward restoring peace after nearly two years of bloody conflict rather than a capitulation to militant demands.

## Background: A Valley Torn by Conflict

The agreement caps roughly 18 months of intense fighting between Pakistani security forces and militants loyal to Maulana Fazlullah, a hardline cleric whose Tehrik-i-Nifaz-i-Shariat-i-Muhammadi (TNSM) movement has waged an insurgency demanding the imposition of strict Islamic law across the once-peaceful tourist region, known for its scenic mountains and ski resorts.

The military offensive, launched in an effort to reclaim territory from militant control, displaced hundreds of thousands of residents, shuttered schools—particularly those educating girls—and left much of the valley's infrastructure in ruins. Human rights organizations documented widespread abuses during the conflict, including summary executions, beheadings, and the destruction of dozens of schools by militants opposed to secular education.

Despite deploying thousands of troops and heavy weaponry, the Pakistani military struggled to decisively defeat the insurgents, who exploited the region's mountainous terrain and, according to analysts, drew strength from cross-border sanctuaries near the Afghan frontier.

## The Deal and Government Justification

Under the agreement, brokered with Sufi Muhammad—the father-in-law of Fazlullah and a longtime advocate for Sharia enforcement in the region—Islamabad has agreed to the establishment of Islamic courts in Swat and the broader Malakand region in exchange for a cessation of hostilities.

Government officials have characterized the move not as surrender, but as a response to longstanding public demand for a faster, more culturally rooted judicial system. Provincial officials in North-West Frontier Province argued that Pakistan's civil courts have long been criticized locally for corruption and years-long delays, and that qazi courts—Islamic tribunals—could deliver swifter justice while undercutting the militants' primary rallying cry.

"This is about giving people what they have wanted for decades," one provincial government spokesperson said, emphasizing that the Sharia system to be implemented would operate within the framework of Pakistan's constitution, with appeals still possible through the national judiciary.

Officials also framed the truce as a necessary pause to allow displaced civilians to return home and for humanitarian access to resume, insisting that military options remain available should militants violate the agreement's terms or continue attacks on security forces.

## Skepticism at Home and Abroad

The agreement has drawn sharp criticism from Western governments and independent analysts, who warn it may simply hand the Taliban and allied militants a sanctuary to regroup, much as similar peace deals in Pakistan's tribal areas collapsed in years past, followed by renewed and often deadlier violence.

Critics also point out that Fazlullah's forces have shown little indication of disarming, and that the ceasefire does little to address the network of militant training camps believed to be operating in the region. Women's rights advocates have raised alarms that formalizing Sharia courts could further erode protections for women and girls, building on the damage already done by school closures and threats against female teachers and students during the fighting.

Pakistani officials, however, have pushed back against suggestions that the deal represents a broader capitulation to extremism, insisting it is a localized, targeted arrangement aimed at separating the population's legitimate grievances from the militants' violent agenda.

## Uncertain Road Ahead

Whether the truce holds remains an open question. Previous ceasefires in Pakistan's northwest have proven fragile, often unraveling within months as militant factions used lulls in fighting to consolidate power. For now, the government insists it is committed to monitoring compliance, though it has offered few specifics on enforcement mechanisms should the agreement break down.

As displaced families begin trickling back into Swat's war-scarred towns, the durability of the peace—and the precedent it sets for other restive regions along the Afghan border—will likely determine whether this ceasefire marks a genuine turning point or merely another pause in a much longer struggle.

*This article reflects reporting based on the 2009 Swat Valley peace agreement between the Pakistani government and pro-Taliban cleric Sufi Muhammad.*

# Pakistan's Swat Ceasefire: Zardari Defends Deal Amid Growing Crisis

**Analysis**

Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari has mounted a public defense of a controversial peace agreement with Taliban militants in the Swat Valley, arguing the deal represents pragmatic governance rather than capitulation to extremism. But the ceasefire has drawn sharp criticism at home and abroad as reports of human rights abuses mount and questions grow about whether the accord cedes effective control of the region to militant forces.

## The Deal

The agreement, brokered with pro-Taliban cleric Sufi Muhammad, allows for the implementation of Islamic law—Nizam-e-Adl—in Swat and the broader Malakand region in exchange for a halt to militant violence that has devastated the once-popular tourist valley for nearly two years. The area has seen schools burned, beheadings, and the displacement of hundreds of thousands of residents amid fighting between security forces and militants loyal to Maulana Fazlullah.

## Zardari's Defense

Writing in a widely circulated op-ed, Zardari framed the ceasefire not as surrender but as a calculated attempt to restore order and separate reconcilable elements from hardened militants.

"We are not negotiating with terrorists," Zardari wrote, "but reaching out to citizens who have been terrorized."

He argued that the deployment of Islamic law through legitimate constitutional channels—rather than through Taliban fiat—undercuts the militants' core justification for violence. "By adopting a system of speedy justice through the constitutional process, we are able to address the legitimate grievances of the people of Swat while isolating the terrorists who have used violence and intimidation," he wrote.

Zardari also sought to reassure Western allies wary that Pakistan was abandoning the fight against extremism, insisting the government remained committed to confronting militancy. "The problem of terrorism and militancy is a cancer within Pakistan," he wrote, adding that the state would not tolerate parallel systems of governance that undermine the writ of the state.

## The Fallout

Despite Zardari's assurances, the deal has been met with deep skepticism:

- **Human rights concerns**: Reports from Swat describe public floggings, executions, and the imposition of strict social codes under militant enforcement, raising questions about whether the ceasefire has merely formalized Taliban authority rather than curbing it.

- **Displacement crisis**: Aid organizations report that hundreds of thousands of residents remain displaced, with many unable or unwilling to return despite the supposed truce, citing continued insecurity.

- **U.S. and international alarm**: American officials have expressed concern that the agreement cedes territory to militants just miles from Islamabad, potentially creating a safe haven that could be exploited by al Qaeda-linked networks operating along the Afghan border.

- **Domestic political criticism**: Opposition figures and secular commentators have accused Zardari's government of weakness, warning that the deal sets a precedent for further concessions as militants push into adjacent districts like Buner and Dir.

## The Bigger Picture

The Swat agreement underscores the central dilemma facing Islamabad: how to respond to an insurgency that has proven resistant to military force alone, without appearing to legitimize the very extremism the state claims to oppose. Critics argue that Zardari's rhetorical distinction between "terrorists" and "terrorized citizens" may collapse in practice, particularly if militant commanders retain de facto control over local enforcement.

For now, the ceasefire holds, but tenuously—and its ultimate test will be whether it produces genuine stability or merely a pause before renewed conflict, in Swat and beyond.

*This report reflects developments as of the initial ceasefire period; the situation remained fluid in subsequent months.*
